sections.title: What is Combinatorics?
sections.content:
Combinatorics is the mathematics of counting. 'In how many ways can you arrange n items?' 'How many paths from A to B in a grid?' 'How many binary strings of length n have exactly k ones?' These questions appear throughout DSA in DP problems, probability problems, and standalone counting problems. The core toolkit: permutations (ordered arrangements), combinations (unordered selections), Pascal's triangle, inclusion-exclusion, and stars and bars.

The bridge from combinatorics to implementation is **modular arithmetic**. Combinatorial answers grow factorially - the number of permutations of 20 items exceeds 10^18. Problems almost always ask for the answer modulo 10^9+7. This means you cannot compute the raw count and then mod it - you must mod intermediate results throughout. Division under mod requires modular inverse (from number theory), making that topic a prerequisite.

Pascal's triangle is the practical tool for computing combinations (nCr) when n is small to moderate (up to ~1000). Each entry is `C[i][j] = C[i-1][j-1] + C[i-1][j]`, built bottom-up in O(n^2) time and space. For larger n, precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to the maximum needed value, then answer each C(n, k) query in O(1) using `fact[n] * invFact[k] % MOD * invFact[n-k] % MOD`.

Combinatorics appears in DP problems more than it appears as a standalone topic. Counting paths in a grid is DP where the recurrence is exactly Pascal's rule. Counting the number of BSTs with n nodes is the Catalan number formula. Recognizing the combinatorial identity behind a DP state often lets you jump directly to the O(1) closed-form answer instead of building a full DP table.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use combinatorics when the problem asks to count the number of ways to do something: arrange items, choose a subset, distribute identical items into bins, count paths in a grid, or count sequences with a specific property. The strongest signal is 'mod 10^9+7' combined with a counting question. Inclusion-exclusion applies when you need to count items satisfying 'at least one of several conditions' and the intersections are easy to compute. Stars and bars applies to distributing identical items into distinct bins.
signals: distribute n items into k bins

sections.title: Permutations, Combinations, Pascal's Triangle, Inclusion-Exclusion, and Stars and Bars
sections.content:
## Permutations and Combinations

**Permutation P(n, k)**: ordered arrangements of k items from n. `P(n, k) = n! / (n-k)!`.

**Combination C(n, k)**: unordered selections of k items from n. `C(n, k) = n! / (k! * (n-k)!)`. Also written nCr or "n choose k".

**Key identities**:
- `C(n, k) = C(n, n-k)` - choosing k to include equals choosing n-k to exclude
- `C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1`
- `C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k)` - **Pascal's rule**: either include the nth item or do not

## Pascal's Triangle

Build the nCr table bottom-up using Pascal's rule. `C[0][0] = 1`. For each row i and column j: `C[i][j] = C[i-1][j-1] + C[i-1][j]`. Take mod at each step to prevent overflow.

For queries where n can be very large (up to 10^6), precompute factorials:
```
fact[0] = 1
fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
invFact[n] = modPow(fact[n], MOD-2, MOD)  // Fermat's little theorem
invFact[i] = invFact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD   // fill backwards
C(n, k) = fact[n] * invFact[k] % MOD * invFact[n-k] % MOD
```

## Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion

To count elements satisfying **at least one** of several conditions:

`|A + B| = |A| + |B| - |A intersect B|`

`|A + B + C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A intersect B| - |A intersect C| - |B intersect C| + |A intersect B intersect C|`

Pattern: **add odd-size intersections, subtract even-size intersections**. For k conditions, iterate over all 2^k subsets. If the subset size is odd, add. If even, subtract.

## Stars and Bars

Count ways to place n identical items into k distinct bins: `C(n + k - 1, k - 1)`.

Equivalently: count non-negative integer solutions to `x1 + x2 + ... + xk = n`: `C(n + k - 1, k - 1)`.

With lower bounds `xi >= li`: substitute `yi = xi - li`, reduce to the base case.

IMPORTANT: Stars and bars only works when items are **identical**. For distinct items, the count is different.

## Catalan Numbers

`Cn = C(2n, n) / (n + 1)`

Appear in: number of valid bracket sequences of length 2n, number of distinct BSTs with n nodes, number of triangulations of a convex (n+2)-gon, and number of paths in a grid that do not cross the diagonal.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: The factorial precomputation fills the array forward, then fills inverse factorials backward using the recurrence invFact[i] = invFact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD, requiring only one modular exponentiation for invFact[maxN]. BigInt prevents silent precision loss in intermediate multiplications.

items.name: Catalan Numbers
items.description: The nth Catalan number Cn = C(2n, n) / (n+1) counts valid bracket sequences of length 2n, distinct BSTs with n nodes, and triangulations of convex polygons. Recognizing that a DP recurrence produces Catalan numbers lets you jump to the O(1) closed form instead of building a full DP table.

items.name: Lucas' Theorem for Large n
items.description: When n is large and p is a small prime, C(n, k) mod p equals the product of C(ni, ki) mod p where ni and ki are the digits of n and k in base p. Breaks a large nCr query into small ones. Used in competitive programming when n can be up to 10^18 but p is a small prime.

items.name: Stirling and Bell Numbers
items.description: Stirling numbers of the second kind S(n, k) count the number of ways to partition n distinct items into exactly k non-empty subsets. Bell number B(n) is the total number of partitions of n items. Appear in problems about grouping or partitioning distinct objects.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n^2) to build Pascal's triangle up to size n. O(n) to precompute factorials up to n. O(1) per nCr query after precomputation.
sections.space: O(n^2) for Pascal's triangle. O(n) for factorial and inverse factorial arrays.
sections.explanation: Pascal's triangle has O(n^2) entries, each computed in O(1), giving O(n^2) total. Factorial precomputation is a single linear pass: O(n). Inverse factorial is also O(n): one modular exponentiation for invFact[maxN], then a linear backward pass. After precomputation, each C(n, k) query is three multiplications mod MOD: O(1).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Factorial overflow without mod: `20!` is approximately 2.4 x 10^18, exceeding Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. Always mod intermediate factorial computations. Computing `fact[n]` first and then taking mod at the end loses precision on all intermediate values.

Division under mod requires modular inverse: C(n, k) mod p cannot be computed as `(fact[n] / (fact[k] * fact[n-k])) % p`. Division in modular arithmetic requires multiplying by the modular inverse. Direct division silently produces wrong answers for large n.

Lucas' theorem required when n is very large: for n up to 10^18 and prime p, the standard factorial approach does not work. Lucas' theorem decomposes the query digit by digit in base p. Forgetting this produces wrong answers or memory limit exceeded.

Sign errors in inclusion-exclusion: odd-size intersections are added, even-size intersections are subtracted. Off-by-one in the subset iteration accidentally includes or excludes terms with wrong signs.

Stars and bars only for identical items: the formula C(n+k-1, k-1) counts distributions of n identical balls into k bins. For distinct balls, the count is k^n. Using stars and bars for distinct items gives a completely wrong answer.

items.title: Unique Paths
items.why: Grid path counting reduces to C(m+n-2, m-1): you must take exactly m-1 down steps and n-1 right steps in some order. Direct application of the combination formula, bypassing the DP table entirely.

items.title: Pascal's Triangle
items.why: Direct Pascal's triangle construction. Tests the recurrence C[i][j] = C[i-1][j-1] + C[i-1][j] and correct boundary initialization.

items.title: K-th Symbol in Grammar
items.why: The kth symbol in the nth row can be determined by the parity of the number of 1-bits in k-1. Tests whether you recognize the mathematical pattern rather than simulating exponentially large strings.

items.title: Count Sorted Vowel Strings
items.why: Count strings of length n using 5 vowels in non-decreasing order. This is stars and bars: placing n vowels into 5 ordered bins = C(n+4, 4). Tests recognition of the stars and bars pattern from a problem that does not explicitly mention it.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Matrix algorithms are the next topic in the Others track. Matrix exponentiation - raising a transition matrix to the nth power using fast power - directly combines the fast exponentiation technique from number theory with linear algebra. It computes the nth term of any linear recurrence (including Fibonacci) in O(k^3 log n) where k is the state size.
